Name: Candi Borobudur
Motif: Lotus (repeated throughout); Kala; Naga; Jataka scenes
Associated Object (fill out the object e: Lotus-capital bronze lamp (Nalanda); Stone relief panel with lotus pond (Amaravati)
Associated story/iconography: Life of the Buddha; Jataka tales; Avatamsaka Sutra; cosmological mandala
Analytical Description (150-250 words): Candi Borobudur is the world's largest Buddhist monument, constructed under the Shailendra dynasty on the Kedu Plain of Central Java between roughly 780 and 840 CE. The structure takes the form of a terraced pyramid surmounted by a large stupa, encoding a three-dimensional mandala of the Buddhist cosmos. The lotus motif pervades every level of the monument: thousands of carved panels show the seated Buddha atop a lotus throne, while the water basin surrounding the original site echoed the lotus pond imagery found in earlier South Asian Buddhist narrative reliefs. The iconographic programme draws heavily on South Asian sources—Amaravati relief conventions, Pala-period sculpture types, and Gupta-era Buddha images—refracted through a distinctly Javanese aesthetic sensibility. Borobudur's construction coincided with the height of Srivijayan maritime power, which controlled the Strait of Malacca and facilitated the movement of monks, merchants, and religious objects between India and the Indonesian archipelago. The monument thus stands as a material record of the deep entanglement of South and Southeast Asian Buddhist cultures.
References: Miksic, John. Borobudur: Golden Tales of the Buddhas. Boston: Shambhala, 1990. | Gomez, Luis and Hiram Woodward, eds. Barabudur: History and Significance of a Buddhist Monument. Berkeley: Berkeley Buddhist Studies, 1981. | Dumarçay, Jacques. Borobudur. Oxford: OUP, 1978.
Further Readings: Sundberg, Jeffrey. 'The Wilderness Monks of the Abhayagirivihāra and the Origins of Sino-Javanese Esoteric Buddhism.' Bijdragen tot de Taal-, Land- en Volkenkunde 160, no. 1 (2004): 95–123.

Name: Nalanda Mahavihara (monastic complex)
Patron(s): Gupta rulers; Pala rulers; various donors
Other Associated People: Xuanzang (Chinese pilgrim, 7th c.); Yijing (Chinese pilgrim, 7th c.); Atisha (11th c.)
Motif: Lotus (architectural tile, sculpture); Stupa; Votive objects
Associated Object (fill out the object e: Terracotta lotus tile (Nalanda); Lotus-capital bronze lamp
Analytical Description (150-250 words): Nalanda Mahavihara was the pre-eminent centre of Buddhist learning in South Asia from roughly the 5th to the 12th century CE, attracting students and scholars from across Asia. The complex comprised dozens of monasteries, temples, and libraries arranged around a central processional axis. Excavations have yielded vast quantities of terracotta lotus tiles, bronze votive objects, and clay seals, many of which show iconographic and stylistic parallels with contemporaneous sites in Southeast Asia, suggesting systematic transmission of visual culture through the movement of monks and pilgrims. Chinese pilgrims Xuanzang (629–645 CE) and Yijing (671–695 CE) left detailed accounts of the monastery's scale and cosmopolitan community, noting students from Java, Sumatra, and China. Nalanda thus functioned as both a physical and intellectual hub within the broader Monsoon Asia network, with its architectural vocabulary—including the lotus-decorated plinth—carried to sites as distant as Paharpur (Bangladesh) and Sriksetra (Myanmar) by departing monks and craftspeople.

Further Readings: Liu, Xinru. Ancient India and Ancient China: Trade and Religious Exchanges, AD 1–600. Delhi: OUP, 1988.

column44: Neak Pean (Coiled Serpents) is a small artificial island temple set within a large reservoir (the Northern Baray) at Angkor, constructed under Jayavarman VII in the late 12th century CE. Its circular island is encircled by two intertwined naga serpents whose tails form the temple's base—giving the site its name—and is set within a square pool connected by four subsidiary pools to the four cardinal directions. Each subsidiary pool is accessed through a stone animal head (horse, elephant, lion, human) from which water originally flowed, representing the four sacred rivers of Buddhist cosmology emanating from the Himalayan lake Anavatapta. The site thus encodes an entire Buddhist cosmological landscape in architectural form, with the nagas functioning simultaneously as physical support, cosmological guardian, and embodiment of water's healing power. A celebrated sculptural group on the island's east side depicts Avalokiteshvara in the form of the horse Balaha rescuing shipwrecked sailors from a sea of demons—an image that resonates powerfully with the maritime orientation of the Jayavarman VII building programme and the lived experience of a court dependent on the Tonle Sap's waters. Neak Pean is one of the most eloquent examples in all of Southeast Asian art of the Buddhist absorption and transformation of naga cosmology.

Name: Ajanta Cave 19 (chaitya hall)
Date: late 5th century CE (c. 475–500 CE, Vakataka period)
Other Associated People: Local naga community (textual references); Vakataka court
Motif: Naga (chaitya facade); Buddha (interior apsidal shrine); mithuna; yaksha; lotus
Associated story/iconography: Naga as local guardian deity; Buddhist absorption of pre-existing naga shrine; Muchalinda protection narrative
Analytical Description (150-250 words): Cave 19 at Ajanta is a chaitya (worship hall) of the late Vakataka period, notable for its elaborately carved facade in which naga figures occupy prominent positions flanking the main entrance and appear in the decorative friezes above. Robert Decaroli's research on naga imagery at Ajanta has argued persuasively that the caves were constructed at a site already associated with local naga worship, and that the prominent display of naga imagery on Cave 19's facade functioned as a deliberate address to this pre-existing devotional community—drawing local naga devotees into the Buddhist sacred complex by depicting their tutelary spirits in a position of honour. Inside, the chaitya terminates in a large stupa with a carved Buddha figure, and the interior pillars carry painted and carved narratives including scenes from the Jataka tales. The cave's horseshoe-arch window floods the interior with dramatic light, an effect calculated to enhance the luminous quality of the gilded and painted surfaces. Cave 19 is thus a paradigmatic example of how Buddhist monastic architecture in South Asia strategically incorporated local devotional traditions—particularly naga veneration—into its spatial and iconographic programme, a strategy documented across Monsoon Asia from Ajanta to Angkor.
References: Decaroli, Robert. "The Abode of the Naga King: Questions of Art, Audience, and Local Deities at the Ajanta Caves." Ars Orientalis 40 (2011): 142–161. | Cohen, Richard. "Nāga, Yakṣiṇī, Buddha: Local Deities and Local Buddhism at Ajanta." History of Religions 37, no. 4 (1998): 360–400. | Spink, Walter M. Ajanta: History and Development. 7 vols. Leiden: Brill, 2005–2014.
Further Readings: Dehejia, Vidya. Indian Art. London: Phaidon, 1997, pp. 137–152.

Name: Brihadesvara Temple (Rajarajesvaram)
Architect: Kunjara Mallan Raja Raja Perunthachan (traditional attribution)
Other Associated People: Rajendra I (continuation of endowments); devadasi community; Shaiva theologians
Motif: Shiva; Nandi; Nataraja; Dakshinamurti; Bhikshatana; Shaiva cosmology
Associated story/iconography: Shaiva cosmology; Shiva as world teacher (Dakshinamurti); Shiva as dancer (Nataraja); Chola royal legitimation
Analytical Description (150-250 words): The Brihadesvara Temple at Thanjavur, completed by Rajaraja I around 1010 CE, is the culminating monument of the imperial Chola building programme and one of the most ambitious architectural achievements of medieval South Asia. The temple's vimana (tower) rises approximately 66 metres above the Tamil plain, making it the tallest structure in South Asia at the time of its construction. The exterior walls carry an encyclopaedic programme of Shaiva sculptural imagery—Nataraja, Dakshinamurti, Bhikshatana, Ardhanarisvara, and the eight directional guardians—executed in a monumental style that established the canonical grammar of Tamil Shaiva temple sculpture for subsequent centuries. The temple was simultaneously a theological statement, a royal legitimation device, and an economic institution: its endowment inscriptions (some of the longest surviving medieval Tamil texts) record the gifting of thousands of bronzes, land grants, and the installation of hundreds of devadasi and priest communities, making the temple the centre of a vast redistributive economy. The bronze Nataraja images produced for Brihadesvara and its daughter temples were carried by Tamil merchant networks across the Indian Ocean, physically broadcasting Chola cultural and theological authority to courts and communities from Sri Lanka to Southeast Asia.

The Home of Dancing Sivan: The Traditions of the Hindu Temple in Citamparam. Oxford: OUP, 1995. | Pichard, Pierre. Tanjavur Brhadisvara: An Architectural Study. Pondicherry: EFEO, 1994.
Further Readings: Heitzman, James. Gifts of Power: Lordship in an Early Indian State. Delhi: OUP, 1997.

Name: Nagapattinam Buddhist Monastery (Chudamani Vihara)
Date: founded c. 7th century CE; refurbished 11th century CE (largely destroyed by 14th century CE)
Patron(s): Srivijayan king Maravijayottungavarman (11th-century refurbishment); Rajaraja I (land grant)
Other Associated People: Tamil Buddhist monks; Srivijayan monks; John Guy (modern scholar)
Motif: Standing Buddha; Buddhist stupa; lotus; Tamil-Srivijayan syncretic Buddhist iconography
Associated story/iconography: Tamil Buddhist patronage; Srivijayan endowment; cross-cultural Buddhist exchange
Analytical Description (150-250 words): The Chudamani Vihara (Jewel-Crest Monastery) at Nagapattinam was the most important Buddhist monastery on the Coromandel Coast, and one of the most remarkable examples of cross-cultural religious patronage in medieval South Asia. The monastery was substantially refurbished in the 11th century CE by the Srivijayan king Maravijayottungavarman with the explicit permission of the Chola king Rajaraja I—a transaction recorded in a copper plate inscription that reveals the degree to which Srivijayan and Chola elites were enmeshed in a shared economy of Buddhist patronage despite their political rivalry. John Guy has documented the monastery's role as a production centre for the distinctive Nagapattinam bronze Buddhist images—small, highly portable votives bearing Tamil Buddhist iconographic features—that circulated across the Bay of Bengal to Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia, and China. The monastery was destroyed sometime in the 14th century CE, possibly during the period of Vijayanagara expansion, and its site is now occupied by a Jesuit church. Excavations in the 19th and early 20th centuries recovered hundreds of bronze Buddhist images from the monastery's ruins, many of which entered colonial-era museum collections. The Chudamani Vihara thus survives not as architecture but as a dispersed archive of portable objects tracing the deep entanglement of Tamil and Srivijayan Buddhist cultures.

Singapore: ISEAS, 2011. | Kulke, Hermann et al., eds. Nagapattinam to Suvarnadwipa. Singapore: ISEAS, 2009.
Further Readings: Ahilan, Karuppiah. "Political Boundaries or Cultural Zones." (2017).

Analytical Description (150-250 words): Neak Pean (Coiled Serpents) is a small island temple set within a large reservoir at Angkor, constructed under Jayavarman VII in the late 12th century CE. Two intertwined naga serpents encircle the central island, while a square pool connects to four subsidiary pools at the cardinal directions. Each subsidiary pool is accessed through a stone animal head from which water once flowed, representing the four sacred rivers of Buddhist cosmology emanating from the Himalayan lake Anavatapta. The site encodes an entire cosmological landscape in architectural form: the nagas simultaneously support the structure physically, guard its waters spiritually, and embody the healing power associated with Anavatapta in Buddhist texts. A sculptural group on the east side depicts Avalokiteshvara as the horse Balaha rescuing shipwrecked sailors, an image resonating with the maritime orientation of Jayavarman VII's court and the lived experience of a kingdom dependent on the waters of the Tonle Sap. Neak Pean is one of the most eloquent examples in Southeast Asian art of the Buddhist absorption of naga cosmology into monumental sacred space.
